中国China and भारतIndia

Two new nations, two very different paths. Scroll down to compare how China and India developed, decade by decade.

1947 to the early 2000s
1940s–60s

China建国初期

Under the leadership of Mao Zedong, China adopted a centralized communist economy. The state made decisions on all economic choices. The Great Leap Forward was an attempt to industrialize the country but it instead led to a deadly famine. China became reliant on agricultural imports from the Soviet Union. Land redistribution was attempted and had mixed results.

Under the Communist Party, China became a one-party dictatorship that viewed democratic ideas as dangerous. Mao instituted the Cultural Revolution, which led to further economic disruptions.

Indiaस्वतंत्र भारत

Under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, the government adopted a mixed economy with strong state planning. This included Five-Year Plans guided development, major investment in heavy industry (steel, power, machinery), the creation of large public-sector companies, and high tariffs to protect domestic industry.

India’s industrial capabilities grew but economic growth was slow. Agriculture remained a weakness and India relied on imports.

India adopted a democratic form of government with liberal ideologies.

1970s–80s

China改革开放

After Mao's death in 1976, Deng Xiaoping rose to power and began a policy called "Reform and Opening Up" in 1978. Under Deng, China opened Special Economic Zones, such as Shenzhen, that welcomed foreign investment. In these zones, foreign companies could build factories and take advantage of low taxes and cheap labor.

Agriculture also saw deregulation. Under the new household responsibility system, farmers could sell any surplus crops they grew for their own profit, which encouraged them to produce more. Some private businesses were also allowed to open for the first time since the communist takeover. China saw tremendous economic growth due to these reforms, with its economy growing by roughly 10 percent per year during the 1980s.

Indiaसुधार

The Green Revolution was introduced to India, bringing high-yield varieties of wheat and rice along with fertilizers and irrigation. Agricultural output boomed, and by the late 1970s India was producing enough grain to feed itself. However, rural inequality grew, since wealthier farmers could afford the new seeds and equipment while poorer farmers fell behind.

The government still highly regulated the economy through a system nicknamed the “License Raj,” which required businesses to get government permits to open, expand, or import goods. This kept economic growth slow, at about 3–4% per year. In the 1980s, under Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, some tariffs were reduced and a few industries, such as electronics, were deregulated.

1990s

China九十年代

China focused on manufacturing and exports. The state heavily invested in infrastructure and factories, which led to China becoming the “World’s Factory” by the end of the 1990s.

As a result, China saw rapid urbanization. Cities like Shenzhen went from a fishing village of a couple thousand people in 1980 to a city of several million by the late 1990s.

Indiaउदारीकरण

The 1991 Economic Crisis forced massive reforms in India. Tariffs were reduced further and deregulation expanded. Privatization of industries and foreign investment also increased significantly.

India focused primarily on service industries like software development, finance, and information technologies. Manufacturing grew slowly as a result.

2000s

China新世纪初

After joining the World Trade Organization in 2001, China had one of the fastest sustained growth rates in history, with its economy often growing 8–10% per year for decades. Hundreds of millions of people were lifted out of extreme poverty as factory and city jobs replaced rural farming.

The government also funded a large infrastructure expansion, building new ports, railways, and highways, including the world’s largest high-speed rail network. In 2010, China passed Japan to become the second largest economy in the world. Today it is a major global investor and infrastructure builder, funding roads, ports, and railways in countries across Asia, Africa, and beyond.

Indiaनई सदी

India’s economic growth accelerated after 1991, often reaching 6–8% per year, and remained steady into the 2000s. Cities like Bangalore became global centers for software and technology companies. Poverty declined significantly, but more gradually than in China, and millions of people still live in poverty, especially in rural areas.

Infrastructure such as highways, airports, and telecommunications improved, but the improvements were uneven across the country, with large cities developing much faster than rural regions. After passing the United Kingdom in 2022 and Japan more recently, India’s economy is currently the fourth largest in the world and is still growing.
